claim: The study performed in vitro whole-cell recordings from up to eight excitatory neurons simultaneously.
source: We performed in vitro whole-cell recordings from up to eight excitatory neurons simultaneously.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section describing the experimental methodology.

claim: The study probed 2836 putative connections in mouse V1 from excitatory cell classes defined by transgenic labeling, morphology, and cortical layer.
source: We probed 2836 putative connections in mouse V1 from excitatory cell classes defined by transgenic labeling, morphology, and cortical layer (Tasic et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section reporting the number of connections tested.

claim: The study probed 616 putative connections in human frontal and temporal cortex from excitatory cell classes defined by morphology and cortical layer.
source: We further probed 616 putative connections in human frontal and temporal cortex from excitatory cell classes defined by morphology and cortical layer (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section reporting the number of connections tested in human tissue.

claim: Recurrent connectivity was tested and observed in layer 2/3 through layer 6 of mouse primary visual cortex.
source: Recurrent connectivity was tested and observed in layer 2/3 through layer 6 of mouse primary visual cortex and layer 2 through layer 6 of the human cortex.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section describing the layers examined.

claim: Recurrent connectivity was tested and observed in layer 2 through layer 6 of the human cortex.
source: Recurrent connectivity was tested and observed in layer 2/3 through layer 6 of mouse primary visual cortex and layer 2 through layer 6 of the human cortex.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section describing the layers examined in human cortex.

claim: Connections were identified by the presence of excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) evoked with a short latency and low jitter following the presynaptic spike, consistent with monosynaptic connections.
source: Connections were identified by the presence of excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) evoked with a short latency and low jitter following the presynaptic spike, consistent with monosynaptic connections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement describing the criteria for identifying connections, with reference to supporting figure.

claim: No examples of EPSPs eliciting spikes in any recorded pyramidal cells were encountered.
source: We encountered no examples of EPSPs eliciting spikes in any recorded pyramidal cells, further indicating that evoked polysynaptic activity should be rare in these experiments.
evidence: Direct statement of an observation from the experiments.

claim: The absence of EPSPs eliciting spikes indicates that evoked polysynaptic activity should be rare in these experiments.
source: We encountered no examples of EPSPs eliciting spikes in any recorded pyramidal cells, further indicating that evoked polysynaptic activity should be rare in these experiments.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that EPSPs did not elicit spikes.

claim: For >75% of the recorded cells, a biocytin fill was recovered.
source: For >75% of the recorded cells, we recovered a biocytin fill (Figure 1A) and for all cells we obtained an epifluorescent image stack (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement about the recovery rate of biocytin fills, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: For all recorded cells, an epifluorescent image stack was obtained.
source: For >75% of the recorded cells, we recovered a biocytin fill (Figure 1A) and for all cells we obtained an epifluorescent image stack (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement about obtaining epifluorescent images for all cells, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners in mouse cortex.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the total number of connections detected in mouse cortex.

claim: In mouse layer 2/3, 15 connections were detected.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections detected in layer 2/3.

claim: In mouse Rorb neurons, 20 connections were detected.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections detected in Rorb neurons.

claim: In mouse Tlx3 neurons, 39 connections were detected.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections detected in Tlx3 neurons.

claim: In mouse Sim1 neurons, 55 connections were detected.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections detected in Sim1 neurons.

claim: In mouse Ntsr1 neurons, 2 connections were detected.
source: Connections were detected between 131 putative pre- and post-synaptic partners (layer 2/3: 15, Rorb: 20, Tlx3: 39, Sim1: 55, Ntsr1: 2; Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections detected in Ntsr1 neurons.

claim: A majority of the connections had amplitudes less than 0.5 mV.
source: Consistent with previous reports that recurrent connectivity is weak (Song et al., 2005; Lefort et al., 2009), we found that a majority of the connections had amplitudes less than 0.5 mV.
evidence: Direct statement about the amplitude distribution of connections, with citation to previous work.

claim: Previous reports indicate that recurrent connectivity is weak.
source: Consistent with previous reports that recurrent connectivity is weak (Song et al., 2005; Lefort et al., 2009), we found that a majority of the connections had amplitudes less than 0.5 mV.
evidence: Citation to previous studies reporting weak recurrent connectivity.

claim: There was no statistical difference in the EPSP amplitudes between groups (KW p=0.07).
source: In this small sample, we did not observe statistical difference in the EPSP amplitudes (Figure 1E,F) between groups (KW p=0.07), although there was a trend toward overall smaller Tlx3 EPSP amplitudes (median ± SD 0.14 ± 0.24 mV).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result comparing EPSP amplitudes across groups.

claim: There was a trend toward overall smaller Tlx3 EPSP amplitudes (median ± SD 0.14 ± 0.24 mV).
source: In this small sample, we did not observe statistical difference in the EPSP amplitudes (Figure 1E,F) between groups (KW p=0.07), although there was a trend toward overall smaller Tlx3 EPSP amplitudes (median ± SD 0.14 ± 0.24 mV).
evidence: Direct statement about a trend in the data with specific amplitude values.

claim: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 connections spanned 0.032–0.902 mV.
source: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 (0.032–0.902 mV), Rorb (0.105–1.626 mV), Sim1 (0.068–1.254 mV), and Tlx3 (0.02–0.833 mV) spanned an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 connections.

claim: The range of amplitudes for Rorb connections spanned 0.105–1.626 mV.
source: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 (0.032–0.902 mV), Rorb (0.105–1.626 mV), Sim1 (0.068–1.254 mV), and Tlx3 (0.02–0.833 mV) spanned an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the range of amplitudes for Rorb connections.

claim: The range of amplitudes for Sim1 connections spanned 0.068–1.254 mV.
source: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 (0.032–0.902 mV), Rorb (0.105–1.626 mV), Sim1 (0.068–1.254 mV), and Tlx3 (0.02–0.833 mV) spanned an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the range of amplitudes for Sim1 connections.

claim: The range of amplitudes for Tlx3 connections spanned 0.02–0.833 mV.
source: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 (0.032–0.902 mV), Rorb (0.105–1.626 mV), Sim1 (0.068–1.254 mV), and Tlx3 (0.02–0.833 mV) spanned an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the range of amplitudes for Tlx3 connections.

claim: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3, Rorb, Sim1, and Tlx3 connections spanned an order of magnitude.
source: The range of amplitudes for layer 2/3 (0.032–0.902 mV), Rorb (0.105–1.626 mV), Sim1 (0.068–1.254 mV), and Tlx3 (0.02–0.833 mV) spanned an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the range of amplitudes across connection types.

claim: The amplitude and relatively long latency of Ntsr1 connections are consistent with connections between corticothalamic (CT) layer six neurons in the rat cortex.
source: We could not assess the range of recurrent Ntsr1 connections due to the low number of connections measured; however, the amplitude and relatively long latency (Figure 1F) are consistent with connections between corticothalamic (CT) layer six neurons in the rat cortex (West et al., 2006; Table 1).
evidence: Comparison of observed properties with previous findings in rat cortex, with citation.

claim: The mean EPSP amplitude was consistently larger than the median.
source: The mean EPSP amplitude was consistently larger than the median (Table 2) due to a skewed (long-tailed) distribution of response amplitudes.
evidence: Direct statement about the relationship between mean and median amplitudes, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The mean EPSP amplitude being larger than the median is due to a skewed (long-tailed) distribution of response amplitudes.
source: The mean EPSP amplitude was consistently larger than the median (Table 2) due to a skewed (long-tailed) distribution of response amplitudes.
evidence: Explanation of the statistical observation based on the distribution shape.

claim: Similar observations in the rat visual cortex and mouse somatosensory cortex have led to the suggestion that rare, large-amplitude connections are important for reliable information processing.
source: Similar observations in the rat visual cortex, and mouse somatosensory cortex, has led to the suggestion that rare, large-amplitude connections are important for reliable information processing (Song et al., 2005; Lefort et al., 2009; Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous studies that made similar observations and interpretations.

claim: The majority of EPSP latencies were less than 2.5 ms.
source: The majority of EPSP latencies were less than 2.5 ms (Table 2), and similar across populations (KW p=0.17), consistent with a direct, monosynaptic connection between recorded neurons.
evidence: Direct statement about latency measurements with reference to Table 2.

claim: EPSP latencies were similar across populations (KW p=0.17).
source: The majority of EPSP latencies were less than 2.5 ms (Table 2), and similar across populations (KW p=0.17), consistent with a direct, monosynaptic connection between recorded neurons.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result comparing latencies across populations.

claim: The observed EPSP latencies are consistent with a direct, monosynaptic connection between recorded neurons.
source: The majority of EPSP latencies were less than 2.5 ms (Table 2), and similar across populations (KW p=0.17), consistent with a direct, monosynaptic connection between recorded neurons.
evidence: Interpretation of the latency data as supporting monosynaptic connections.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of each connection describes the variability in a particular response in relation to the mean and is negatively correlated with release probability.
source: The CV of each connection describes the variability in a particular response in relation to the mean (ratio of standard deviation to mean) and is negatively correlated with release probability (Markram, 1997).
evidence: Definition of CV and its relationship to release probability, with citation.

claim: The range of coefficient of variation in the data suggests differences in release probability between cell classes.
source: The range of coefficient of variation in our data suggests differences in release probability between cell classes and is consistent with STP modeling results (see Figure 6).
evidence: Interpretation of CV data as indicating differences in release probability, with reference to modeling results.

claim: The range of coefficient of variation is consistent with STP modeling results.
source: The range of coefficient of variation in our data suggests differences in release probability between cell classes and is consistent with STP modeling results (see Figure 6).
evidence: Statement that CV data are consistent with modeling results, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Human specimens were collected during surgical resection of epileptic or tumorous tissue, but were distal to the site of pathology.
source: Specimens were collected during surgical resection of epileptic or tumorous tissue, but were distal to the site of pathology.
evidence: Direct statement about the source and characteristics of human tissue specimens.

claim: The study sampled recurrent intralayer connectivity in all layers containing pyramidal cells in human cortex.
source: We sampled recurrent intralayer connectivity in all layers containing pyramidal cells.
evidence: Direct statement about the sampling strategy in human cortex.

claim: Pyramidal cells in human cortex were identified by their morphology visualized via biocytin or fluorescent dye.
source: Pyramidal cells were identified by their morphology visualized via biocytin (Figure 2A) or fluorescent dye (Figure 2B).
evidence: Direct statement about the method for identifying pyramidal cells, with references to figures.

claim: In human layer 2, 22 connections were found out of 132 probed.
source: We found 22 connections between layer 2 pyramidal cells (132 probed), 37 connections between layer 3 pyramidal cells (249 probed), four connections between layer 4 pyramidal cells (123 probed), and 13 connections between layer 5 pyramidal cells (112 probed).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections found and probed in human layer 2.

claim: In human layer 3, 37 connections were found out of 249 probed.
source: We found 22 connections between layer 2 pyramidal cells (132 probed), 37 connections between layer 3 pyramidal cells (249 probed), four connections between layer 4 pyramidal cells (123 probed), and 13 connections between layer 5 pyramidal cells (112 probed).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections found and probed in human layer 3.

claim: In human layer 4, four connections were found out of 123 probed.
source: We found 22 connections between layer 2 pyramidal cells (132 probed), 37 connections between layer 3 pyramidal cells (249 probed), four connections between layer 4 pyramidal cells (123 probed), and 13 connections between layer 5 pyramidal cells (112 probed).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections found and probed in human layer 4.

claim: In human layer 5, 13 connections were found out of 112 probed.
source: We found 22 connections between layer 2 pyramidal cells (132 probed), 37 connections between layer 3 pyramidal cells (249 probed), four connections between layer 4 pyramidal cells (123 probed), and 13 connections between layer 5 pyramidal cells (112 probed).
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections found and probed in human layer 5.

claim: In human layer 6, 1 connection was found out of 16 probed connections.
source: We found 1 connection in layer 6 (16 probed connections) but have not yet probed this layer sufficiently to make confident measurements of connection probability or synaptic properties.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of connections found and probed in human layer 6.

claim: Human layer 6 has not yet been probed sufficiently to make confident measurements of connection probability or synaptic properties.
source: We found 1 connection in layer 6 (16 probed connections) but have not yet probed this layer sufficiently to make confident measurements of connection probability or synaptic properties.
evidence: Direct statement about the limitations of the data for human layer 6.

claim: 1.3 mM [Ca++]e was selected for human experiments because of reports that synaptic strength is higher than in mouse.
source: We selected 1.3 mM [Ca++]e for our human experiments because of reports that synaptic strength is higher than in mouse and to minimize the complex events that can be initiated by individual spikes in human tissue (Molnár et al., 2008) that make identifying monosynaptic connectivity challenging.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for the calcium concentration used, with citation.

claim: 1.3 mM [Ca++]e was selected for human experiments to minimize the complex events that can be initiated by individual spikes in human tissue that make identifying monosynaptic connectivity challenging.
source: We selected 1.3 mM [Ca++]e for our human experiments because of reports that synaptic strength is higher than in mouse and to minimize the complex events that can be initiated by individual spikes in human tissue (Molnár et al., 2008) that make identifying monosynaptic connectivity challenging.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for the calcium concentration used, with citation.

claim: Human cortex had a higher connectivity rate compared to mouse cortex.
source: Indeed we found that human cortex had a higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude (Figure 2C,D) compared to mouse cortex (despite a higher [Ca++]e in mouse), consistent with previous reports (Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct statement comparing connectivity rates between human and mouse, with reference to figures and citation.

claim: Human cortex had a higher mean amplitude compared to mouse cortex.
source: Indeed we found that human cortex had a higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude (Figure 2C,D) compared to mouse cortex (despite a higher [Ca++]e in mouse), consistent with previous reports (Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct statement comparing mean amplitudes between human and mouse, with reference to figures and citation.

claim: Human cortex had a higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude compared to mouse cortex despite a higher [Ca++]e in mouse.
source: Indeed we found that human cortex had a higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude (Figure 2C,D) compared to mouse cortex (despite a higher [Ca++]e in mouse), consistent with previous reports (Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct statement comparing connectivity and amplitude between species, noting the calcium concentration difference.

claim: The finding that human cortex has higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude is consistent with previous reports.
source: Indeed we found that human cortex had a higher connectivity rate and mean amplitude (Figure 2C,D) compared to mouse cortex (despite a higher [Ca++]e in mouse), consistent with previous reports (Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement that the findings are consistent with previous work, with citation.

claim: Human layers 2, 3, and 5 had a sufficient number of connections to characterize strength and kinetics.
source: Layers 2, 3, and 5 had a sufficient number of connections to characterize strength and kinetics.
evidence: Direct statement about which layers had sufficient data for analysis.

claim: No differences in response properties were found among human layers 2, 3, and 5 (amplitude p=0.22, latency p=0.51, rise time p=0.22).
source: However, we found no differences in response properties among these three layers (amplitude p=0.22, latency p=0.51, rise time p=0.22, Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results comparing response properties across human layers.

claim: Differences in CV were observed between human layers 2, 3, and 5 (p=0.0004).
source: We did observe differences in CV between layers 2, 3, and 5 (p=0.0004, Table 3) suggesting layer-specific differences in release probability of recurrent connections, similar to findings in mouse V1.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result showing differences in CV across human layers.

claim: Differences in CV between human layers 2, 3, and 5 suggest layer-specific differences in release probability of recurrent connections.
source: We did observe differences in CV between layers 2, 3, and 5 (p=0.0004, Table 3) suggesting layer-specific differences in release probability of recurrent connections, similar to findings in mouse V1.
evidence: Interpretation of CV differences as indicating layer-specific differences in release probability.

claim: The layer-specific differences in release probability in human cortex are similar to findings in mouse V1.
source: We did observe differences in CV between layers 2, 3, and 5 (p=0.0004, Table 3) suggesting layer-specific differences in release probability of recurrent connections, similar to findings in mouse V1.
evidence: Comparison of human findings with mouse findings.

claim: It is reasonable to question if the recurrent connectivity in tissue from epilepsy and tumor patients differs from that of healthy individuals.
source: It is reasonable to question if the recurrent connectivity we see in tissue from epilepsy and tumor patients differs from that of healthy individuals.
evidence: Acknowledgment of a potential limitation or concern about the human tissue source.

claim: No significant differences in overall connectivity were seen between tumor and epilepsy-derived specimens (p=0.833, Fisher's Exact Test).
source: Although we cannot rule this out, we saw no significant differences in overall connectivity between tumor and epilepsy-derived specimens (p=0.833, Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result comparing connectivity between tissue sources.

claim: Recurrent connections were found within multiple cortical regions and disease states in the human.
source: We also found recurrent connections within multiple cortical regions and disease states in the human.
evidence: Direct statement about the distribution of findings across regions and disease states.

claim: The results may indicate that recurrent connectivity captures a common architecture of the mouse and human microcircuit.
source: Taken together, this may indicate that our results capture a common architecture of the mouse and human microcircuit.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings as suggesting a common architecture across species.

claim: When using whole cell recordings to characterize synaptic connectivity, a major limitation is that some EPSPs may be too weak to be detected at the postsynaptic soma.
source: When using whole cell recordings to characterize synaptic connectivity, a major limitation is that some EPSPs may be too weak to be detected at the postsynaptic soma.
evidence: Direct statement about a limitation of the experimental method.

claim: Detection limits are influenced by several factors including the kinetics of EPSPs, the amplitude and kinetics of background noise, the frequency and properties of spontaneous EPSPs, and the number of evoked presynaptic spikes.
source: Detection limits are influenced by several factors including the kinetics of EPSPs, the amplitude and kinetics of background noise, the frequency and properties of spontaneous EPSPs, and the number of evoked presynaptic spikes.
evidence: Direct statement listing factors that influence detection limits.

claim: One consequence of detection limits is that connectivity is expected to be generally underestimated.
source: One consequence is that we expect to generally underestimate connectivity, and in some cases, cell class differences in synaptic strength can be misinterpreted as differences in connectivity.
evidence: Direct statement about a consequence of detection limits.

claim: Cell class differences in synaptic strength can be misinterpreted as differences in connectivity.
source: One consequence is that we expect to generally underestimate connectivity, and in some cases, cell class differences in synaptic strength can be misinterpreted as differences in connectivity.
evidence: Direct statement about a potential misinterpretation arising from detection limits.

claim: It may not be possible to obtain an accurate measurement of the distribution of synaptic weights, since the weakest synapses are undetectable.
source: Another consequence is that it may not be possible to obtain an accurate measurement of the distribution of synaptic weights, since the weakest synapses are undetectable.
evidence: Direct statement about another consequence of detection limits.

claim: The sensitivity of experiments was characterized by testing whether a machine classifier could detect simulated EPSPs of varying, known strength.
source: To address these issues, we characterized the sensitivity of our experiments by testing whether a machine classifier could detect simulated EPSPs of varying, known strength (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: Direct statement describing the method used to characterize detection sensitivity.

claim: The classifier was trained to detect connections based on features extracted from the averaged response to evoked spikes and from the distributions of features measured on individual responses.
source: The classifier was trained to detect connections based on features extracted from the averaged response to evoked spikes (Figure 3B; features listed in Supplementary file 1) and from the distributions of features measured on individual responses (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement describing the classifier training approach, with references to figures and supplementary file.

claim: By testing several sets of artificial EPSPs in which the average amplitude was systematically varied, the relationship between EPSP strength and the probability that a connection could escape detection was measured.
source: By testing several sets of artificial EPSPs in which we systematically varied the average amplitude, we were able to measure the relationship between EPSP strength and the probability that a connection could escape detection (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement describing the method for measuring detection probability, with reference to figure.

claim: The analysis provides, for every connection that was probed, an estimate of the minimum detectable EPSP amplitude.
source: This analysis provides, for every connection that we probed, an estimate of the minimum detectable EPSP amplitude (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct statement about the output of the detection limit analysis, with reference to figure.

claim: Recordings with low background noise and adequate averaging will generally allow the detection of very small EPSPs (detection limit of 10–20 µV).
source: Recordings with low background noise and adequate averaging will generally allow the detection of very small EPSPs (Figure 3D, top panel has a detection limit of 10–20 µV), whereas lower quality recordings will have higher detection thresholds and will report lower connectivity rates (Figure 3D, bottom panel has a poor detection limit near 100 µV).
evidence: Direct statement about detection limits under different recording conditions, with reference to figure.

claim: Lower quality recordings will have higher detection thresholds and will report lower connectivity rates (detection limit near 100 µV).
source: Recordings with low background noise and adequate averaging will generally allow the detection of very small EPSPs (Figure 3D, top panel has a detection limit of 10–20 µV), whereas lower quality recordings will have higher detection thresholds and will report lower connectivity rates (Figure 3D, bottom panel has a poor detection limit near 100 µV).
evidence: Direct statement about detection limits under different recording conditions, with reference to figure.

claim: EPSPs with shorter rise time are more likely to be detected.
source: Likewise, EPSPs with shorter rise time (or other properties that distinguish the EPSP from background) are more likely to be detected (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement about the effect of EPSP kinetics on detection probability, with reference to figure.

claim: Differences in experimental protocol between studies can have a substantial impact on the apparent connectivity reported.
source: These results confirm that the differences in experimental protocol between studies (for example, the number of presynaptic spikes evoked for each connection) can have a substantial impact on the apparent connectivity reported, but also suggests that future studies could reconcile these differences by carefully characterizing their detection limits.
evidence: Interpretation of the detection limit analysis results.

claim: Future studies could reconcile differences in reported connectivity by carefully characterizing their detection limits.
source: These results confirm that the differences in experimental protocol between studies (for example, the number of presynaptic spikes evoked for each connection) can have a substantial impact on the apparent connectivity reported, but also suggests that future studies could reconcile these differences by carefully characterizing their detection limits.
evidence: Suggestion for how to address variability in connectivity measurements across studies.

claim: Dividing the measured distribution of EPSP amplitudes by the probability of detection yields a corrected distribution with an overall 10% increase in connectivity.
source: Dividing the measured distribution by the probability of detection yields a corrected distribution (dark grey) with an overall 10% increase in connectivity.
evidence: Direct statement about the result of correcting for detection probability.

claim: The left edge of the corrected distribution trends downward even in the region where detection probability is high, suggesting that the sensitivity of experiments is adequate to capture the majority of synapses.
source: Although this estimate becomes unstable as the detection probability nears zero, an interesting result is that the left edge of the distribution trends downward even in the region where detection probability is high, suggesting that the sensitivity of our experiments is adequate to capture the majority of synapses and that we have accurately represented the underlying distribution of synaptic strengths.
evidence: Interpretation of the corrected distribution as indicating adequate experimental sensitivity.

claim: The corrected distribution suggests that the underlying distribution of synaptic strengths has been accurately represented.
source: Although this estimate becomes unstable as the detection probability nears zero, an interesting result is that the left edge of the distribution trends downward even in the region where detection probability is high, suggesting that the sensitivity of our experiments is adequate to capture the majority of synapses and that we have accurately represented the underlying distribution of synaptic strengths.
evidence: Interpretation of the corrected distribution as indicating accurate representation of synaptic strengths.

claim: The analysis of the corrected distribution relies on several assumptions about the behavior of the classifier and the realism of the simulated EPSPs.
source: We are cautious, however, in our interpretation of this result--the analysis relies on several assumptions about the behavior of the classifier and the realism of the simulated EPSPs.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations and assumptions in the analysis.

claim: The approach for estimating the distribution of synaptic strengths must be validated against a larger dataset.
source: Ultimately, the approach must be validated against a larger dataset.
evidence: Statement about the need for further validation of the method.

claim: Estimates of connectivity vary widely across studies, in part due to methodological differences.
source: Estimates of connectivity vary widely across studies, in part due to methodological differences.
evidence: Direct statement about variability in connectivity estimates across studies.

claim: Estimated connection probability is affected by the intersomatic distances over which connections are sampled.
source: In addition to the effects of detection sensitivity described above, estimated connection probability is affected by the intersomatic distances over which connections are sampled.
evidence: Direct statement about a factor affecting connectivity estimates.

claim: The spatial distribution of connections may offer insight into the organization of functional microcircuits.
source: This spatial distribution of connections may also offer insight into the organization of functional microcircuits.
evidence: Statement about the potential significance of spatial connectivity patterns.

claim: In mouse, connectivity in layer 2/3, Rorb, and Sim1 neurons within 100 µm was similar (~10%).
source: In mouse, connectivity in layer 2/3, Rorb, and Sim1 neurons within 100 µm was similar (~10%; Figure 4, left; connected/probed, L2/3: 13/130, Rorb: 18/247, Sim1: 41/527).
evidence: Direct statement about connectivity rates within 100 µm for specific cell types, with data and figure reference.

claim: Within 100 µm, Tlx3 connectivity was markedly lower (~5%) than layer 2/3, Rorb, and Sim1.
source: However, within this range, Tlx3 connectivity was markedly lower (~5%; Tlx3: 36/746).
evidence: Direct statement about Tlx3 connectivity rate within 100 µm, with data.

claim: Ntsr1 connectivity was very sparse as only two connections were detected out of 313 probed.
source: Consistent with previous experiments in rat L6 CT neurons (West et al., 2006), Ntsr1 connectivity was very sparse as only two connections were detected (out of 313 probed) and were relatively far apart (intersomatic distance of 163 and 127 µm; Bonferroni corrected p<0.01 relative to all other groups).
evidence: Direct statement about Ntsr1 connectivity with data and statistical comparison, with citation to previous work.

claim: The two detected Ntsr1 connections were relatively far apart (intersomatic distance of 163 and 127 µm).
source: Consistent with previous experiments in rat L6 CT neurons (West et al., 2006), Ntsr1 connectivity was very sparse as only two connections were detected (out of 313 probed) and were relatively far apart (intersomatic distance of 163 and 127 µm; Bonferroni corrected p<0.01 relative to all other groups).
evidence: Direct statement about the distances of the detected Ntsr1 connections.

claim: Ntsr1 connectivity was significantly lower than all other groups (Bonferroni corrected p<0.01).
source: Consistent with previous experiments in rat L6 CT neurons (West et al., 2006), Ntsr1 connectivity was very sparse as only two connections were detected (out of 313 probed) and were relatively far apart (intersomatic distance of 163 and 127 µm; Bonferroni corrected p<0.01 relative to all other groups).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison showing Ntsr1 connectivity is significantly lower.

claim: The sparse Ntsr1 connectivity is consistent with previous experiments in rat L6 CT neurons.
source: Consistent with previous experiments in rat L6 CT neurons (West et al., 2006), Ntsr1 connectivity was very sparse as only two connections were detected (out of 313 probed) and were relatively far apart (intersomatic distance of 163 and 127 µm; Bonferroni corrected p<0.01 relative to all other groups).
evidence: Statement that the findings are consistent with previous work, with citation.

claim: Most connectivity versus distance profiles showed a progressive reduction in the connection probability with increasing distance.
source: Most connectivity versus distance profiles (Figure 4B) showed a progressive reduction in the connection probability with increasing distance.
evidence: Direct statement about the general pattern of connectivity versus distance, with figure reference.

claim: An analysis of reciprocal (bi-directional) connectivity was not carried out because of lack of statistical power to detect differences between classes.
source: We did not carry out an analysis of reciprocal (bi-directional) connectivity because we lacked the statistical power to detect differences between our classes.
evidence: Direct statement explaining why reciprocal connectivity was not analyzed.

claim: Measuring reciprocal connectivity at the cell class level can yield misleading results.
source: Furthermore, measuring reciprocal connectivity at the cell class level can yield misleading results (Hoffmann and Triesch, 2017).
evidence: Statement about a potential problem with measuring reciprocal connectivity, with citation.

claim: Two-photon optogenetic stimulation was used to overcome the limitations of multipatch technique in probing connectivity at high density and long distances.
source: Utilizing a multipatch technique limits our ability to probe connectivity at high density and long distances. We used two-photon optogenetic stimulation to overcome these limitations, which allows for focal stimulation of many (mean = 56 cells, range = 8–117 cells) presynaptic cells in a single experiment, and critically, allows probing distances greater than is generally feasible with multipatch experiments.
evidence: Direct statement about the rationale for using two-photon optogenetics and its advantages.

claim: Two-photon optogenetic stimulation allows for focal stimulation of many presynaptic cells in a single experiment (mean = 56 cells, range = 8–117 cells).
source: Utilizing a multipatch technique limits our ability to probe connectivity at high density and long distances. We used two-photon optogenetic stimulation to overcome these limitations, which allows for focal stimulation of many (mean = 56 cells, range = 8–117 cells) presynaptic cells in a single experiment, and critically, allows probing distances greater than is generally feasible with multipatch experiments.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of cells that can be stimulated with two-photon optogenetics.

claim: With two-photon optogenetics, a similar connection probability was found over the distance range of multipatch experiments (4/136, 2.15%).
source: With this technique, using 12 mice, we found a similar connection probability over the distance range of multipatch experiments (4/136, 2.15%) and reduced connectivity at extended distances up to 785 µm (Figure 4E; 13/1594, 0.82%) with the furthest connection found at 459 µm.
evidence: Direct statement about connectivity measured with two-photon optogenetics at short distances, with data.

claim: With two-photon optogenetics, reduced connectivity was found at extended distances up to 785 µm (13/1594, 0.82%).
source: With this technique, using 12 mice, we found a similar connection probability over the distance range of multipatch experiments (4/136, 2.15%) and reduced connectivity at extended distances up to 785 µm (Figure 4E; 13/1594, 0.82%) with the furthest connection found at 459 µm.
evidence: Direct statement about connectivity measured with two-photon optogenetics at long distances, with data.

claim: The furthest connection found with two-photon optogenetics was at 459 µm.
source: With this technique, using 12 mice, we found a similar connection probability over the distance range of multipatch experiments (4/136, 2.15%) and reduced connectivity at extended distances up to 785 µm (Figure 4E; 13/1594, 0.82%) with the furthest connection found at 459 µm.
evidence: Direct statement about the maximum distance at which a connection was detected.

claim: Short-term dynamics were probed with stimulus trains consisting of 8 pulses to induce STP, followed by a variable delay and 4 more pulses to measure recovery.
source: We probed short-term dynamics with stimulus trains consisting of 8 pulses to induce STP, followed by a variable delay and 4 more pulses to measure recovery (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: Direct statement describing the stimulation protocol for measuring short-term plasticity.

claim: The 8 initial pulses allowed responses to reach a steady state, from which the extent of depression or facilitation at frequencies from 10 to 100 Hz could be characterized.
source: The 8 initial pulses allowed responses to reach a steady state, from which we could characterize the extent of depression (or facilitation) at frequencies from 10 to 100 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for the 8-pulse induction protocol.

claim: The 50 Hz stimulation protocol had additional recovery intervals ranging from 250 to 4000 ms.
source: The 50 Hz stimulation protocol had additional recovery intervals ranging from 250 to 4000 ms (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: Direct statement about the recovery intervals used in the 50 Hz protocol.

claim: A short train of 4 pulses was used to measure recovery to improve sensitivity in modeling the recovered state of the synapse.
source: Although typical experiments use a single delayed pulse to measure recovery, we used a short train of 4 pulses to improve sensitivity in modeling the recovered state of the synapse.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for using 4 recovery pulses instead of 1.

claim: Exponential deconvolution was used to estimate the amplitudes of individual PSPs in the absence of temporal summation.
source: We used exponential deconvolution (Figure 5B, middle; Equation 2) to estimate the amplitudes of individual PSPs in the absence of temporal summation (arising from the relatively long cell membrane time constant).
evidence: Direct statement describing the use of deconvolution to measure PSP amplitudes, with figure and equation reference.

claim: Depression was seen in Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 synapses.
source: Across cell classes we saw depression in Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 synapses, whereas layer 2/3 synapses showed modest facilitation on average (Figure 5C, bottom left).
evidence: Direct statement about the short-term plasticity observed in different cell classes, with figure reference.

claim: Layer 2/3 synapses showed modest facilitation on average.
source: Across cell classes we saw depression in Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 synapses, whereas layer 2/3 synapses showed modest facilitation on average (Figure 5C, bottom left).
evidence: Direct statement about the short-term plasticity observed in layer 2/3, with figure reference.

claim: The two Ntsr1 connections showed facilitation as has been previously reported for layer 6 CT neurons.
source: The two Ntsr1 connections (data not shown) also showed facilitation as has been previously reported for layer 6 CT neurons (West et al., 2006).
evidence: Direct statement about Ntsr1 short-term plasticity, with citation to previous work.

claim: The heterogeneity in layer 2/3 dynamics is highlighted by the amplitude ratio of the last to first pulse, where some synapses depressed strongly and others facilitated.
source: The amplitude ratio of the last pre-recovery pulse (8) to the first, for individual connections (Figure 5D, left), highlights the heterogeneity in layer 2/3 dynamics where some synapses depressed strongly (ratio < 1) and others facilitated (ratio > 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the heterogeneity in layer 2/3 short-term plasticity, with figure reference.

claim: Individual dynamics in Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 generally showed more depression than layer 2/3 (KW p=0.04).
source: Individual dynamics in Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 generally showed more depression than layer 2/3 (KW p=0.04).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison of depression across cell classes.

claim: All types showed a similar time-course of recovery as measured by the ratio of the first recovery pulse to the first induction pulse.
source: All types showed a similar time-course of recovery as measured by the ratio of the first recovery pulse (9) to the first induction pulse (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: Direct statement about the similarity in recovery time-course across cell types, with figure reference.

claim: Previous reports in rat somatosensory cortex showed that recurrent connections between thick tufted layer 5b cortical neurons can facilitate.
source: Although we observed depression in both layer 5 classes, previous reports in rat somatosensory cortex showed that recurrent connections between thick tufted layer 5b cortical neurons can facilitate (Reyes and Sakmann, 1999; Lefort and Petersen, 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous studies reporting facilitation in layer 5 neurons.

claim: The availability of free calcium in the presynaptic terminal impacts release probability and thus short-term dynamics of a synapse.
source: The availability of free calcium in the presynaptic terminal impacts release probability and thus short-term dynamics of a synapse (Rozov et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement about the relationship between calcium and short-term dynamics, with citation.

claim: It was hypothesized that 0.3 mM EGTA in the intracellular solution may buffer presynaptic calcium accumulation and reduce the magnitude of facilitation observed in layer 5 connections.
source: We hypothesized that 0.3 mM EGTA in the intracellular solution may buffer presynaptic calcium accumulation and reduce the magnitude of facilitation observed in our layer 5 connections.
evidence: Direct statement of a hypothesis about the effect of EGTA on short-term plasticity.

claim: In the absence of EGTA, overall depression was seen in both Tlx3 and Sim1 over the course of a 50 Hz train.
source: Over the course of a 50 Hz train, we saw overall depression in both Tlx3 and Sim1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) such that the 8:1 pulse ratio was statistically indistinguishable in the two EGTA concentrations (Tlx3 KS test p=0.47; Sim1 KS test p=0.35; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Table 4).
evidence: Direct statement about short-term plasticity in the absence of EGTA, with statistical test results and figure references.

claim: The 8:1 pulse ratio was statistically indistinguishable in the two EGTA concentrations for Tlx3 (KS test p=0.47) and Sim1 (KS test p=0.35).
source: Over the course of a 50 Hz train, we saw overall depression in both Tlx3 and Sim1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) such that the 8:1 pulse ratio was statistically indistinguishable in the two EGTA concentrations (Tlx3 KS test p=0.47; Sim1 KS test p=0.35; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Table 4).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results comparing EGTA conditions.

claim: Tlx3 synapses show transient facilitation during the second pulse of the train in the absence of EGTA (KS test p=0.04).
source: We did observe, however, that Tlx3 synapses show transient facilitation during the second pulse of the train (paired-pulse ratio; KS test p=0.04; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, top; Table 4).
evidence: Direct statement about paired-pulse facilitation in Tlx3 in the absence of EGTA, with statistical test result and figure reference.

claim: No significant difference in paired-pulse ratio was seen for Sim1 connections in the absence of EGTA (KS test p=0.35).
source: We did not see a significant difference in paired-pulse ratio for Sim1 connections in the absence of EGTA (KS test p=0.35; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, bottom; Table 4).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result for Sim1 paired-pulse ratio, with figure reference.

claim: Tlx3 and Sim1 cell classes have different synaptic dynamics but are nonetheless dominated by depression.
source: This suggests that Tlx3 and Sim1 cell classes have different synaptic dynamics but are nonetheless dominated by depression.
evidence: Interpretation of the EGTA experiments as indicating differences in dynamics between Tlx3 and Sim1.

claim: A model of short-term dynamics with depression and use-dependent replenishment was applied to characterize dynamic processes contributing to short-term plasticity.
source: To more fully capture the dynamic processes contributing to short-term plasticity and how they may differ among connection types we turned to a model of short-term dynamics which has been well described (Hennig, 2013; Mongillo et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 2005).
evidence: Direct statement about the modeling approach used, with citations.

claim: For homogeneous populations, applying the model to an average response will accurately represent the short-term dynamics of a particular cell class.
source: For homogeneous populations, we expect that applying the model to an average response will accurately represent the short-term dynamics of a particular cell class.
evidence: Statement about the expected validity of the modeling approach for homogeneous populations.

claim: Layer 2/3, Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 synapses were modeled with depression and use-dependent replenishment.
source: Layer 2/3, Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1 synapses were modeled with depression (Equation 4, Materials and methods) and use-dependent replenishment (Equation 5, Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement about which cell types were modeled and with which mechanisms.

claim: For the more homogeneous cell classes (Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1), the model performed well in capturing depression and recovery.
source: For the more homogeneous cell classes (Rorb, Tlx3, and Sim1), the model performed well (Figure 6A, Sim1 connections r2 = 0.845, Table 5) in capturing depression during the eight initial pulses at various frequencies (Figure 6A) as well as modeling recovery at various delays for 50 Hz stimuli (Figure 6A, open circles).
evidence: Direct statement about the model performance for specific cell classes, with r-squared value and figure/table references.

claim: Heterogeneity among layer 2/3 synapses made it difficult to constrain the model and thus were not included in further analysis.
source: Heterogeneity among layer 2/3 synapses made it difficult to constrain the model and thus were not included in further analysis.
evidence: Direct statement explaining why layer 2/3 was excluded from modeling analysis.

claim: Rorb connections had the largest release probability (P0 = 0.30).
source: Rorb connections had the largest release probability (P0 = 0.30, Figure 6B, left) which is consistent with faster entry into depression (Figure 5C, bottom pulse 2).
evidence: Direct statement about the modeled release probability for Rorb, with figure references.

claim: The large release probability of Rorb connections is consistent with faster entry into depression.
source: Rorb connections had the largest release probability (P0 = 0.30, Figure 6B, left) which is consistent with faster entry into depression (Figure 5C, bottom pulse 2).
evidence: Interpretation of the modeled release probability as explaining the observed dynamics.

claim: Tlx3 connections had a lower initial release probability (P0 = 0.16) and recovered more quickly (τr0 = 0.736 s).
source: Conversely, Tlx3 connections had a lower initial release probability (P0 = 0.16) and recovered more quickly (𝜏r0 = 0.736 s).
evidence: Direct statement about the modeled parameters for Tlx3 connections.

claim: Sparse recurrent connections were observed between excitatory neurons in layers 2/3 through 6 in adult mouse visual cortex.
source: We observed sparse recurrent connections between excitatory neurons in layers 2/3 through 6 in adult mouse visual cortex and layers 2 through 6 of adult human cortex.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the main finding in mouse cortex.

claim: Sparse recurrent connections were observed between excitatory neurons in layers 2 through 6 of adult human cortex.
source: We observed sparse recurrent connections between excitatory neurons in layers 2/3 through 6 in adult mouse visual cortex and layers 2 through 6 of adult human cortex.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the main finding in human cortex.

claim: Mouse multipatch experiments were supplemented with high-throughput 2P optogenetic stimulation to sample connectivity at greater distances than is generally feasible using the multipatch approach.
source: We supplemented mouse multipatch experiments with high-throughput 2P optogenetic stimulation to sample connectivity at greater distances than is generally feasible using the multipatch approach.
evidence: Direct statement about the use of two-photon optogenetics to extend the distance range.

claim: Most excitatory recurrent connections in mouse cortex were dominated by short-term synaptic depression.
source: Most excitatory recurrent connections in mouse cortex were dominated by short-term synaptic depression.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the main finding about short-term plasticity.

claim: Estimates of connectivity derived from multipatch experiments in brain slices should be considered as a lower bound on the underlying population connectivity due to sensitivity to false negatives from several sources.
source: Estimates of connectivity derived from multipatch experiments in brain slices should be considered as a lower bound on the underlying population connectivity due to sensitivity to false negatives from several sources.
evidence: Direct statement about the interpretation of connectivity estimates from slice experiments.

claim: A fraction of synaptic connections are expected to be severed during slicing; one estimate of connectivity perturbed by slicing approaches 50%.
source: A fraction of synaptic connections are expected to be severed during slicing; one estimate of connectivity perturbed by slicing approaches 50% (Levy and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: Statement about the effect of slicing on connectivity, with citation.

claim: The effect of slicing on measured connection probability depends on the thickness of the slice, the depth of recorded cells from the cut surface, the morphology of recorded cells, and the distance between them.
source: The effect on measured connection probability depends on the thickness of the slice, the depth of recorded cells from the cut surface, the morphology of recorded cells, and the distance between them.
evidence: Statement about factors that influence the effect of slicing on connectivity measurements.

claim: Lost connections due to slicing are minimized by patching deep in the slice (>40 µm) and by selecting cells in close proximity.
source: Although we minimize lost connections by patching deep in the slice (>40 µm; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D) and by selecting cells in close proximity, this is still a likely source of false negatives in our data.
evidence: Direct statement about the strategies used to minimize false negatives from slicing.

claim: Slicing is still a likely source of false negatives in the data despite efforts to minimize lost connections.
source: Although we minimize lost connections by patching deep in the slice (>40 µm; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D) and by selecting cells in close proximity, this is still a likely source of false negatives in our data.
evidence: Acknowledgment that slicing remains a source of false negatives.

claim: Another fraction of synapses are expected to be either too weak or too distal from the recording pipette to be detected.
source: Another fraction of synapses are expected to be either too weak (Isaac et al., 1995) or too distal from the recording pipette to be detected.
evidence: Statement about another source of false negatives, with citation.

claim: The initial analysis hints that the methods are sensitive enough to capture the majority of synapses.
source: The magnitude of this effect is difficult to estimate, but our initial analysis hints that our methods are sensitive enough to capture the majority of synapses.
evidence: Interpretation of the detection limit analysis as suggesting adequate sensitivity.

claim: To obtain more accurate estimates of connectivity, it will be necessary to combine these results with other methods such as in vivo multipatch recordings, transsynaptic tracing, and serial section electron microscopy.
source: To obtain more accurate estimates of connectivity, it will be necessary to combine these results with other methods such as in vivo multipatch recordings, transsynaptic tracing, and serial section electron microscopy.
evidence: Statement about the need for complementary methods to improve connectivity estimates.

claim: Other methods for measuring connectivity are also limited, but in each case the constraints are different and potentially complementary.
source: These methods are also limited, but in each case the constraints are different and potentially complementary.
evidence: Statement about the complementary nature of different methods.

claim: There is a wide range of reported rates of recurrent connectivity among excitatory neurons in rodent studies.
source: There is a wide range of reported rates of recurrent connectivity among excitatory neurons in rodent studies (Thomson et al., 2002; Hofer et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about variability in the literature, with citations.

claim: One suggestion is that differences between the juvenile and adult rodent can explain the variance in reported connectivity rates.
source: One suggestion is that differences between the juvenile and adult rodent can explain the variance (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to a hypothesis about the source of variability in connectivity rates.

claim: Experiments were carried out in the adult (about two months old) cortex to avoid changes associated with development.
source: To avoid changes associated with development, we carried out our experiments in the adult (about two months old) cortex.
evidence: Direct statement about the age of animals used to avoid developmental effects.

claim: The conclusion that recurrent connectivity is sparse but not absent is similar to results from experiments in other adult and juvenile animals.
source: Nevertheless, our conclusion that recurrent connectivity is sparse but not absent is similar to results from experiments in other adult (Reyes and Sakmann, 1999; Lee et al., 2016) and juvenile animals (Mason et al., 1991; Holmgren et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Sjöström et al., 2001; Morishima et al., 2011; Perin et al., 2011; Lefort et al., 2009; Levy and Reyes, 2012; Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement that the findings are consistent with previous work, with multiple citations.

claim: Rates of recurrent connectivity as high or synaptic amplitudes as large as those reported in juvenile rodents were never observed.
source: A notable difference, however, is that we never observed rates of recurrent connectivity as high or synaptic amplitudes as large as those reported in juvenile rodents, consistent with the observation that the rate of recurrent connectivity and synaptic strength declines with age (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1993; Reyes and Sakmann, 1999).
evidence: Direct statement about a difference from juvenile studies, with citations.

claim: The rate of recurrent connectivity and synaptic strength declines with age.
source: A notable difference, however, is that we never observed rates of recurrent connectivity as high or synaptic amplitudes as large as those reported in juvenile rodents, consistent with the observation that the rate of recurrent connectivity and synaptic strength declines with age (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1993; Reyes and Sakmann, 1999).
evidence: Citation to previous work showing age-related decline in connectivity and strength.

claim: All excitatory cell classes investigated in this study, in human and in mouse, exhibited recurrent connectivity.
source: All excitatory cell classes investigated in this study, in human and in mouse, exhibited recurrent connectivity but the rate of recurrent connectivity depended on the class.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the finding that all classes showed recurrent connectivity.

claim: The rate of recurrent connectivity depended on the cell class.
source: All excitatory cell classes investigated in this study, in human and in mouse, exhibited recurrent connectivity but the rate of recurrent connectivity depended on the class.
evidence: Direct statement that connectivity rate varied by cell class.

claim: In two subcortically projecting neuron classes, the connectivity rate was approximately 10% in Sim1 (layer 5) expressing cells.
source: For example, in two subcortically projecting neuron classes, the connectivity rate was approximately 10% in Sim1 (layer 5) expressing cells, whereas Ntsr1 expressing cells (layer 6) had the lowest rate of intralaminar connectivity among all excitatory cell classes tested in this study.
evidence: Direct statement about the connectivity rate in Sim1 cells.

claim: Ntsr1 expressing cells (layer 6) had the lowest rate of intralaminar connectivity among all excitatory cell classes tested in this study.
source: For example, in two subcortically projecting neuron classes, the connectivity rate was approximately 10% in Sim1 (layer 5) expressing cells, whereas Ntsr1 expressing cells (layer 6) had the lowest rate of intralaminar connectivity among all excitatory cell classes tested in this study.
evidence: Direct statement about the connectivity rate in Ntsr1 cells.

claim: The low Ntsr1 connectivity is consistent with previous work on layer 6 CT cells using multipatch and single cell rabies tracing.
source: This low connectivity is consistent with previous work on layer 6 CT cells using multipatch (West et al., 2006) and single cell rabies tracing (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement that the findings are consistent with previous work, with citations.

claim: The results suggest that recurrent connectivity may be a general property of excitatory neurons that is regulated depending on the target region.
source: Our results suggest that recurrent connectivity may be a general property of excitatory neurons that is regulated depending on the target region.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings as suggesting a general property with regulation.

claim: In human cortex, the frequency of connectivity among excitatory neurons is at least two and half times greater than the highest connectivity rate observed in the adult mouse.
source: In human cortex, we and others (Molnár et al., 2008) find that the frequency of connectivity among excitatory neurons is at least two and half times greater than the highest connectivity rate observed in the adult mouse.
evidence: Direct statement comparing human and mouse connectivity rates, with citation.

claim: High rates of recurrent connectivity in human may be a circuit feature of higher mammals as this is also reported to be the case in cat and monkey.
source: It may be that high rates of recurrent connectivity in human are a circuit feature of higher mammals as this is also reported to be the case in cat and monkey (Kisvárday et al., 1986; McGuire et al., 1991; Bopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation about the significance of high human connectivity, with citations to other species.

claim: Another possibility is that the observed difference between mouse and human is more related to the different cortical regions.
source: Another possibility, however, is that the observed difference between mouse and human is more related to the different cortical regions.
evidence: Alternative explanation for the species difference.

claim: Future work will examine how relatively high recurrent connectivity might be counterbalanced by short-term dynamics and/or inhibitory feedback.
source: Future work will examine how relatively high recurrent connectivity might be counterbalanced by short-term dynamics and/or inhibitory feedback.
evidence: Statement about future research directions.

claim: The distance-dependent connection probability profiles fall off with distance and are consistent with connectivity depending on the extent of overlap between neighboring axons and dendrites.
source: In our study, the distance-dependent connection probability profiles fall off with distance and are consistent with connectivity depending on the extent of overlap between neighboring axons and dendrites (Peters, 1979; Binzegger et al., 2004, Braitenberg and Schüz 1998, van Pelt et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement that the observed distance dependence is consistent with anatomical overlap, with citations.

claim: It is unlikely that the distance-dependent connectivity profiles observed are an artifact of tissue preparation.
source: It is unlikely that the distance-dependent connectivity profiles we observed are an artifact of tissue preparation as it has previously been demonstrated that the truncation of neuronal processes reduces overall connectivity but maintains the spatial pattern of connections (Stepanyants et al., 2009; Levy and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: Statement that the distance dependence is not an artifact, with citations to previous work.

claim: The truncation of neuronal processes reduces overall connectivity but maintains the spatial pattern of connections.
source: It is unlikely that the distance-dependent connectivity profiles we observed are an artifact of tissue preparation as it has previously been demonstrated that the truncation of neuronal processes reduces overall connectivity but maintains the spatial pattern of connections (Stepanyants et al., 2009; Levy and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: Citation to previous work showing that slicing maintains spatial patterns.

claim: Further effort is required to determine whether connectivity profiles cannot be predicted from neuronal morphology as has been observed in intralaminar connections between corticostriatal neurons.
source: Further effort is required to determine whether our connectivity profiles cannot be predicted from neuronal morphology as has been observed in, for example, intralaminar connections between corticostriatal neurons (Brown and Hestrin, 2009).
evidence: Statement about the need for further work to determine if morphology alone can predict connectivity, with citation.

claim: The study measured connectivity and synaptic properties within broad cell classes that include multiple subtypes.
source: Like most similar studies (e.g. Mason et al., 1991; Markram, 1997; Sjöström et al., 2001) that have preceded this work, we have measured connectivity and synaptic properties within broad cell classes that include multiple subtypes.
evidence: Direct statement about the level of cell classification used, with citations to similar studies.

claim: Differences between broad cell classes were found, but important cell-type-dependent differences may be obscured by this approach.
source: Although we found differences between these classes, we expect that in some cases, important cell-type-dependent differences will be obscured by this approach.
evidence: Acknowledgment of a limitation of the cell classification approach.

claim: Initially, the distribution of properties can be characterized and related to morphological and electrophysiological properties that relate to narrower cell classes or types.
source: Initially, we can mitigate this by characterizing the distribution of properties and relating these to morphological and electrophysiological properties that relate to narrower cell classes or types.
evidence: Statement about a strategy to address the limitation of broad cell classes.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis has refined and expanded the catalog of cell types, necessitating the development of new methods to measure synaptic properties with greater cell type resolution.
source: However, transcriptomic analysis (Tasic et al., 2016; Chevée et al., 2018) has refined and expanded the catalog of cell types, necessitating the development of new methods to measure synaptic properties with greater cell type resolution and with enough throughput to address the sizeable combinatorial space of connections between types.
evidence: Statement about the need for new methods given advances in cell type classification, with citations.

claim: In the primary visual cortex of the adult mouse, recurrent connections, except for Ntsr1 connections and a subset of L2/3 connections, depressed after eight action potentials across a range of frequencies.
source: In the primary visual cortex of the adult mouse, we found that recurrent connections, except for Ntsr1 connections and a subset of L2/3 connections, depressed after eight action potentials across a range of frequencies.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the short-term plasticity findings.

claim: Although depression dominates the net response, it is important to consider that facilitation, depression, and other mechanisms may simultaneously contribute to overall short-term dynamics.
source: Although depression dominates the net response, it is important to consider that facilitation, depression, and other mechanisms may simultaneously contribute to overall short-term dynamics.
evidence: Statement about the complexity of short-term plasticity mechanisms.

claim: The availability of calcium in the presynaptic terminal can strongly influence the balance between mechanisms in a cell-class-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, the availability of calcium in the presynaptic terminal can strongly influence the balance between mechanisms in a cell-class-dependent manner (e.g., Tlx3 vs. Sim1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement about the effect of calcium on short-term plasticity, with reference to figure showing cell class differences.

claim: Despite differences in intracellular EGTA buffering between this study and others, the STP observed in mouse recurrent synapses is mostly consistent with previous work.
source: Despite differences in intracellular EGTA buffering between our study and others, the STP we observed in mouse recurrent synapses is mostly consistent with previous work (West et al., 2006; Lefort and Petersen, 2017) with the primary exception being the lack of facilitation in paired pulses in layer 5 neurons.
evidence: Statement that the findings are mostly consistent with previous work, with citations, noting one exception.

claim: The primary exception to consistency with previous work is the lack of facilitation in paired pulses in layer 5 neurons.
source: Despite differences in intracellular EGTA buffering between our study and others, the STP we observed in mouse recurrent synapses is mostly consistent with previous work (West et al., 2006; Lefort and Petersen, 2017) with the primary exception being the lack of facilitation in paired pulses in layer 5 neurons.
evidence: Statement about a difference from previous work.

claim: When facilitation was unmasked by lowering the intracellular EGTA concentration it was not in the mouse line with thick-tufted pyramidal neurons (Sim1) as expected from work in other brain regions.
source: Interestingly, when facilitation was unmasked by lowering the intracellular EGTA concentration it was not in the mouse line with thick-tufted pyramidal neurons (Sim1; Gouwens and Berg, 2018) as we expected from work in other brain regions (Reyes and Sakmann, 1999; Lefort and Petersen, 2017), suggesting that the recurrent connectivity STP may differ across brain regions for the same projection class.
evidence: Statement about an unexpected finding regarding facilitation in Sim1 neurons, with citations.

claim: The recurrent connectivity STP may differ across brain regions for the same projection class.
source: Interestingly, when facilitation was unmasked by lowering the intracellular EGTA concentration it was not in the mouse line with thick-tufted pyramidal neurons (Sim1; Gouwens and Berg, 2018) as we expected from work in other brain regions (Reyes and Sakmann, 1999; Lefort and Petersen, 2017), suggesting that the recurrent connectivity STP may differ across brain regions for the same projection class.
evidence: Interpretation of the unexpected finding as suggesting regional differences in STP.

claim: A comprehensive description of cortical networks requires a large-scale, systematic approach.
source: Generating a comprehensive description of cortical networks requires a large-scale, systematic approach.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract about the need for systematic approaches.

claim: A pipeline project using multipatch electrophysiology, supplemented with two-photon optogenetics, has been begun to characterize connectivity and synaptic signaling between classes of neurons in adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and human cortex.
source: To that end, we have begun a pipeline project using multipatch electrophysiology, supplemented with two-photon optogenetics, to characterize connectivity and synaptic signaling between classes of neurons in adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and human cortex.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract describing the project.

claim: The focus is on producing results detailed enough for the generation of computational models and enabling comparison with future studies.
source: We focus on producing results detailed enough for the generation of computational models and enabling comparison with future studies.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract about the goals of the project.

claim: Connections are sparse but present among all excitatory cell classes and layers sampled.
source: We find that connections are sparse but present among all excitatory cell classes and layers we sampled, and that most mouse synapses exhibited short-term depression with similar dynamics.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: Most mouse synapses exhibited short-term depression with similar dynamics.
source: We find that connections are sparse but present among all excitatory cell classes and layers we sampled, and that most mouse synapses exhibited short-term depression with similar dynamics.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract summarizing the short-term plasticity findings.

claim: Synaptic signaling between a subset of layer 2/3 neurons exhibited facilitation.
source: Synaptic signaling between a subset of layer 2/3 neurons, however, exhibited facilitation.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract about an exception to the general pattern of depression.

claim: These results contribute to a body of evidence describing recurrent excitatory connectivity as a conserved feature of cortical microcircuits.
source: These results contribute to a body of evidence describing recurrent excitatory connectivity as a conserved feature of cortical microcircuits.
evidence: Direct statement from the Abstract about the significance of the findings.
